title: Tisha B'Av
hookLine: on the ninth of Av, Jews mourn the destruction of the Temples and read Lamentations

lines: LIGHTS LOW, PEOPLE ON THE FLOOR.
cards: A summer evening. In a synagogue the lights are low. Some people are sitting on the floor or on low stools, the way mourners sit at a shiva.
Nobody greets each other with the usual warmth. Someone begins to read from a short book of poems, in a slow, falling chant.
On this one day of the year, a whole community sits like a family at a funeral, for a loss that happened long before anyone in the room was born. The day is called Tisha B'Av.

teach.h: THE NINTH OF AV, A DAY OF FASTING.
teach.b: First, the date. Tisha B'Av is the ninth of the Jewish month of Av.

The Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish teaching, lists the calamities tradition remembers on that day, among them the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem, the first time and the second. It is kept as a fast.
Second, the book. The reading is Lamentations, short poems of grief for Jerusalem. A few days ago, this path heard a turn in its third chapter; this reading starts at the beginning.
Its Hebrew name is its first word, Eikhah: how.

In the King James Bible it opens, "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow!" Your line today says it in plain modern words: how lonely sits the city. Third, the picture.
The poet doesn't describe rubble. The city becomes a woman sitting alone, a widow, weeping in the night with no one to comfort her. Grief that is too big for a list of facts gets a body and a face.
That may be why the book still works: a person can sit beside a person. Fourth, the ending.

teach.h: RENEW OUR DAYS AS OF OLD.
teach.b: The last chapter turns to a plea: "Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old." Then one more verse, bitter, about being rejected.
In the synagogue, the custom is to repeat the plea for renewal after it, so the reading does not end in the dark. Nothing is fixed. Nobody pretends the loss didn't happen.
But the community grieves out loud, together, on a set day, and then rises from the floor.

how: On Tisha B'Av, observant Jews fast, sit low as mourners do, and hear Lamentations (Eikhah) chanted in the synagogue; the plea 'renew our days as of old' is repeated at the end of the reading.

practice: Read the opening verse once more, slowly, and let it stand for whatever it stands for today: a place you lost, a home that changed, a loss people around you carry, or simply a people who have read these words in grief for a very long time.
No need to fix anything; sit beside it.
